lead: Negative feedback subtracts a measured part of the output from the input. It lets an inaccurate forward path behave more accurately, because the loop corrects what the forward path gets wrong. The price is lower forward gain. The same idea gives closed-loop gain, loop gain and sensitivity, and it changes gain, bandwidth, disturbance rejection, noise and stability. Op-amp circuits, motor speed controls and inverter voltage loops holding 230 V use it.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for open-loop and closed-loop control and the meaning of a summing junction.

blocks.text: In the block diagram, R(s) is the reference input and C(s) is the output. The feedback path measures C(s) and returns B(s) = H(s)C(s). The summing junction forms the error E(s) = R(s) − B(s). The forward path has gain G(s).

Negative feedback uses the minus sign. The equations are C = G E and E = R − H C. Substitute: C = G(R − H C). Bring C terms together: C(1 + GH) = G R. Divide by R: A(s) = C(s)/R(s) = G(s)/(1 + G(s)H(s)).

blocks.where: A is the closed-loop transfer function; G is the forward-path transfer function; H is the feedback-path transfer function; GH is the loop gain. All are functions of s.

blocks.text: GH is the loop gain. The factor 1 + GH is the desensitivity factor D. For the figure, G = 100 and H = 0.1, so GH = 10 and D = 11. The closed-loop gain is A = 100/11 = 9.0909. The forward gain fell from 100 to about 9.09.
With unity feedback H = 1, A = G/(1 + G). If the summing sign is positive, the denominator becomes 1 − GH; that is positive feedback.
A small change in G changes A. Differentiate A = G/(1 + GH) with H fixed. dA/dG = 1/(1 + GH)². Divide by A: dA/A = [1/(1 + GH)] (dG/G).

blocks.where: dA/A is the fractional change in closed-loop gain; dG/G is the fractional change in forward gain; S is the sensitivity of A with respect to G; GH is the loop gain. S is also called the fractional change ratio in some syllabi.

blocks.text: S = 1/D = 1/(1 + GH). For G = 100 and H = 0.1, S = 1/11 = 0.0909. A 10% change in G gives an estimated change in A of 0.0909 × 10% = 0.909%. The estimate is for a small change; it is good for a few percent.

High loop gain makes S small. If GH = 100, S ≈ 0.0099 and A ≈ 1/H for H fixed. The output then depends mostly on H, not G. Feedback does not remove dependence on H: if the sensor gain H drifts, A changes directly. In unity feedback, A = G/(1 + G) and S = 1/(1 + G).

items: Overall gain: A is smaller than G by the factor D = 1 + GH. This is the gain sacrificed for accuracy.

Bandwidth: for a first-order forward path G = K/(1 + sτ) with unity feedback, the closed-loop pole is at −(1 + K)/τ. Bandwidth rises by about 1 + K; gain falls by the same factor, so gain × bandwidth is roughly constant.
Disturbance: a disturbance added inside the loop before the output is attenuated by about 1 + GH at low frequency. A disturbance added after the measurement point is not reduced.
Noise: feedback cannot separate sensor noise from the true output. Noise in H is fed back and can appear at the output; it is not automatically cancelled.

Stability: the closed-loop poles are roots of 1 + G(s)H(s) = 0. Feedback can make a slow system faster and less sensitive, but it can also reduce phase margin and cause oscillation. Stability tests come in Unit 3.
Positive feedback: with a plus sign at the summing junction, A = G/(1 − GH). It increases gain and usually drives the system toward saturation or instability.

blocks.text: Feedback reduces the effect of changes in G, not changes in H. It also does not make C exactly equal R; a nonzero error remains unless the loop gain is infinite at that frequency.

figure.caption: A forward path with G = 100 and feedback H = 0.1; the loop gain is 10, so the closed-loop gain falls to 100/11 ≈ 9.09. Notice the minus sign at the summing junction.

spec.aria: A negative-feedback loop with forward gain 100 and feedback factor 0.1; the feedback path returns to the summing junction with a minus sign.

examples.question: A negative-feedback loop has forward gain G = 100 and feedback factor H = 0.1. (a) Find the closed-loop gain A and the sensitivity S. (b) If G increases by 10%, estimate the percentage change in A.
examples.answer: A = 9.0909; S = 0.0909; a 10% rise in G gives about a 0.909% rise in A.
examples.check:
G = 100.0
H = 0.1
D = 1.0 + G * H
A = G / D
S = 1.0 / D
dG_fraction = 0.10
dA_fraction = S * dG_fraction
print(round(A, 4))
print(round(S, 4))
print(round(dA_fraction * 100, 3))

traps: Using 1 + GH when the summing junction has a plus sign; positive feedback uses 1 − GH.
Saying feedback makes C exactly equal R. It only reduces the error; finite loop gain leaves a steady-state error.
Treating S as sensitivity to H. The formula S = 1/(1 + GH) is sensitivity of A to G.
Forgetting that S is a small-change ratio; for a 10% change the exact change differs slightly.
Assuming feedback always improves stability. It can reduce phase margin; check 1 + GH = 0 in Unit 3.

quiz.q: Define loop gain and desensitivity for a negative-feedback loop.
quiz.a: Loop gain is GH. Desensitivity is D = 1 + GH.

quiz.q: Why does negative feedback reduce the effect of a change in G?
quiz.a: Because dA/A = S dG/G and S = 1/(1 + GH) is less than 1 when GH is positive. The loop corrects part of the change in G.

quiz.q: A negative-feedback loop has G = 50 and H = 0.2. Find A and S.
For GH much greater than 1, A ≈ 1/H. What does this mean for component tolerance?
quiz.a: The closed-loop gain is set mainly by H. An accurate H gives an accurate A even if G varies, provided G is large enough.

quiz.q: A loop has GH = 9. G rises by 20%. Estimate the percentage change in A.
Write the closed-loop gain formula for positive feedback.
Can negative feedback make a stable plant unstable? Explain briefly.
quiz.a: Yes. The closed-loop poles are roots of 1 + GH = 0. Feedback changes the poles and can reduce phase margin. If the loop phase reaches −180° with |GH| ≥ 1, the closed loop is unstable.

quiz.q: Write A and S for unity negative feedback.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, feedback amplifiers, motor drives and power converters are designed by choosing the loop gain GH(s) to meet sensitivity, disturbance rejection and stability margins. The same sensitivity idea extends to state feedback, where a gain vector closes the loop around the plant; see Unit 6. Modern loop-shaping and H-infinity methods shape the sensitivity function directly. Search next for loop gain, sensitivity function, gain-bandwidth trade-off and Bode sensitivity integral.
